content:
Overview

A new joint report from BusinessLDN and CBRE sets out a stark reality for London’s affordable housing market. Despite a £39 billion, 10 year Social and Affordable Housing Programme and a renewed political focus on delivery, affordable housing starts in the capital have collapsed and public sector delivery capacity is now structurally constrained. The conclusion is clear. Without large scale private investment, London will not meet its housing needs.


Delivery Has Fallen Off A Cliff

Affordable housing starts in London peaked at 25,658 homes in 2022 to 2023. In the following year, starts fell by 90 percent to just 2,358 homes, with similarly weak delivery continuing into 2025. This collapse is compounding a long standing structural undersupply and driving record spending on temporary accommodation, now costing London boroughs approximately £5.5 million per day.


Housing Associations Are Financially Constrained

Registered Providers remain central to the affordable housing system, but their balance sheets are under increasing pressure. Across London’s largest housing associations, cash reserves are falling, interest cover ratios are declining, debt levels are rising, and repair, retrofit, fire safety and decarbonisation programmes are absorbing capital. Development pipelines are being reduced. The sector now spends almost £10 billion per year maintaining existing stock. Development investment is falling and asset sales are increasing as providers prioritise financial resilience over growth. This is forcing a shift away from large scale delivery.


The Section 106 Delivery Model Is Breaking Down

Section 106 agreements have historically delivered around 44 percent of all new affordable homes in England. That model is now under strain. Developers are increasingly unable to secure Registered Provider partners to acquire completed affordable units. As a result, schemes are stalling, construction is being delayed, and developers are setting up their own for profit Registered Providers simply to keep sites moving. The impact is now being felt across London’s entire residential development pipeline.


Private Capital Is Already Stepping In

The most visible signal of change is the rapid growth of for profit Registered Providers. There are now 79 for profit providers registered nationally, owning more than 46,500 affordable homes. In London alone, their portfolios have grown by more than 800 percent in six years. In 2025, for profit providers accounted for around 20 percent of all new affordable housing growth. Institutional capital is increasingly acquiring rental tenures, not just shared ownership, positioning affordable housing as a long income investment class.


Affordable Housing Is Now A Long Income Infrastructure Asset

The report frames affordable housing as a structurally undersupplied, policy backed income sector with demand that is resilient across economic cycles. Government backed rent frameworks, long term settlements and indexation provide a foundation for long duration cashflow. However, viability remains constrained by high land and construction costs, rising finance costs, regulatory burdens, and delivery risk within development pipelines. What the sector needs is capital that is structured for long term ownership and supported by robust risk transfer.


The Parx Perspective

Affordable housing is rapidly becoming one of the UK’s most important long income real estate sectors. Demand is permanent, supply is structurally constrained and public funding alone is no longer sufficient. Private capital is now essential to unlock stalled residential schemes, stabilise development pipelines, reduce reliance on temporary accommodation, and deliver the scale of homes London requires. For institutional investors, lenders and developers, the opportunity is clear. The challenge is structuring income certainty, covenant resilience and long term cashflow security around delivery. This is where insurance led risk transfer and long income protection frameworks will play an increasingly central role in shaping the next phase of affordable housing investment.
